# Add A2UI support on top of AG-UI for structured chat rendering #55
...
## Problem

The current chat UI mostly treats assistant output as plain text. AG-UI gives us the runtime/event transport, but it does not by itself provide richer generative UI rendering. This is why long assistant outputs still show up as text bubbles instead of structured UI blocks.

## Goal

Introduce an A2UI-capable rendering path on top of the existing AG-UI integration so agents can return structured UI payloads that render as supported application components instead of plain prose.

## Scope

- keep AG-UI as the transport/runtime layer
- add an A2UI-aware output path for supported assistant responses
- preserve plain-text rendering as the fallback path
- avoid arbitrary uncontrolled UI; only render from an explicit supported component registry

## Proposed Plan

### 1. Audit the current AG-UI message/event path

- document what AG-UI events the backend already emits
- identify where assistant text is normalized into the currentChatMessage model
- identify the narrowest insertion point for structured UI payloads without breaking existing chat history

### 2. Define the supported A2UI surface for this app

Start with a constrained first wave instead of trying to support every possible widget shape.
Recommended first-class renderables:

- tool activity/status cards
- plans/checklists
- file/diff summary cards
- structured lists/tables
- approval/action panels if needed later

Explicitly out of scope for the first pass:

- arbitrary free-form HTML
- iframe-style open-ended widgets
- unrestricted custom component injection

### 3. Add backend/session guidance for A2UI usage

- update session/system instructions so the agent knows when to emit A2UI instead of prose
- define when plain text is still preferred vs when structured UI should be emitted
- make the instructions specific enough that the model does not randomly alternate between text and UI for the same use case

Questions to answer in implementation:

- should this be enabled for all agents or only selected backends first?
- should A2UI capability be tied to backend capability/configuration?
- do we want a per-session or global feature flag while rolling it out?

### 4. Extend the backend output pipeline

- accept and forward A2UI payloads through the AG-UI stream
- normalize structured assistant payloads into a frontend-consumable model
- preserve plain text messages and mixed text+UI payloads
- make parsing failures non-fatal and fall back to plain text

### 5. Add a frontend renderer layer

- extend the chat message renderer so assistant responses can render either:
- markdown/plain text
- A2UI structured content
- mixed content blocks

- build a safe renderer registry for the supported widget types
- ensure unsupported or malformed A2UI payloads degrade gracefully

Suggested frontend pieces:

- StructuredAssistantMessage renderer
- small component registry/mapping layer
- explicit fallback/error boundary for malformed structured payloads

### 6. Integrate with the current chat shell

- ensure structured UI renders well inside the slimmer chat area
- support interaction alongside the composer and workspace modes
- make sure files/diff/project manager flows do not visually conflict with structured assistant UI blocks

### 7. Persistence and replay

- ensure stored session history can replay structured assistant messages correctly
- decide whether to persist raw A2UI payloads, normalized render trees, or both
- verify that reloads and route-based session restoration preserve the rendered UI

### 8. Validation and regression coverage

Add tests for:

- plain text assistant response still rendering normally
- valid structured A2UI response rendering correctly
- malformed A2UI payload falling back safely
- mixed text + structured UI responses
- replaying/restoring structured UI from saved sessions
- interactions inside supported structured widgets if applicable

## Definition of Done

- at least one supported A2UI payload type renders end-to-end through the real chat flow
- plain text chat continues to work unchanged
- malformed structured payloads do not break the conversation UI
- structured responses survive session reload/replay
- tests cover both structured and fallback rendering paths

## Suggested rollout strategy

- start behind a feature flag
- enable for one backend/agent first
- ship with a very small supported component set
- expand once the event model and renderer boundaries feel stable

## Follow-up work

- richer diff/file widgets rendered as structured UI instead of text summaries
- tool execution cards and streaming tool output blocks
- approval/interrupt UI for human-in-the-loop flows
- broader A2UI component support once the minimal path is stable

results.summary:
# 用四大章节，总结AI智能体交互设计的高频问题
...
和传统交互不同，AI 智能体的设计处处藏着 “反常识” 的坑：精心设计的表单，使用体验却很割裂；花心思做的图文混排卡片，反而让对话逻辑变得混乱；自以为贴心的预输入提示词，要么被用户忽略，要么限制了真实需求的表达…
...
在为 AI Agent 做界面设计时，你是否也遇到过这个问题：

#### 1. 主流样式分为两种，气泡式和直铺式：

气泡包裹式（Bubble-style）

最常见于对话型产品，如：豆包、智谱清言、讯飞星火，视觉上接近微信、QQ 等“社交聊天”，一问一答排列，每条内容被圆角容器包裹，可加头像、动效、时间戳等

文本直铺式（Plain-text layout）

更常见于工具型产品，如：chatgpt、gemini、腾讯元宝，视觉上没有明显的聊天结构，直接展示回答；页面结构更接近文章/摘要/模块列表。

两种样式背后的「交互心智」
...
到底什么时候选哪种？

我们来看看设计选型时常见的判断维度：

产品角色：工具型 vs 助理型

工具型（例如搜索总结/导购/智能填表） → 直铺式更合适

助理型（例如问诊机器人、写作助手） → 气泡更适合拟人感和语境延续

内容长度与结构性

长段落、图文混排、有标题层级 → 直铺更清晰

轻量问答、短句型内容 → 气泡更沉浸

多轮对话 vs 单轮回应

多轮交互需要保留上下文 → 气泡逻辑更自然

单轮提问或静态结果展示 → 直铺更高效

是否需拟人感

希望营造“陪伴感” → 拟人气泡配合动效最佳

强调“结果准确” → 工具页面、信息块式表达更稳妥

#### 3. 设计细节建议

气泡建议最大宽度不超过屏宽的 80%-90%，避免读起来太“挤”；问和答的气泡从颜色和长度上都要有所区分；通常问的气泡极值宽度是答的气泡宽度的 90%，这是因为

- 突出重点： 用户的提问是起点，但重点是AI的回答。窄气泡让用户快速浏览自己的问题，把注意力集中在更重要的回答上。
- 便于阅读： AI的回答通常更长、信息量更大。用更宽的气泡可以减少文字换行，让用户读起来更顺畅，体验更好。
- 视觉区分： 窄气泡和宽气泡的对比，能清晰地区分“用户输入”和“AI输出”，让整个对话界面更有条理、一目了然。

可适当加入“正在输入中”的过渡动画，增强沉浸感。这点可以借鉴微信，因为 AI 在进行长回复的时候，是需要等待时间的，这段时间就可以增加“回复中”的 lottie 动画来模拟对方正在回复的感觉，减少等待焦虑。

气泡顶部可添加头像/名称/身份标签，强化 Agent 形象（相对应的可能会降低屏效）

直铺式建议配合 emoji 表情、模块标题、分段逻辑，避免视觉疲劳。
...
大多数用户在第一次和 AI Agent 对话时，都会卡在同一个问题：“我该问点啥？”为了避免用户“开不了口”，几乎所有对话产品都会提供一些「预设提问」或「推荐问题」来降低门槛。
...
降低认知门槛 —— 给用户一个“先开口”的理由

缩短冷启动时间 —— 避免用户盯着空白输入框

引导产品价值呈现 —— 推荐内容就是「产品能帮你做什么」的直观展现

维持对话节奏 —— 用推荐追问延续语境，避免对话突然断掉
...
常见的预设输入机制样式

常见的预设输入样式有 快捷提问、智能追问、预填建议三种类型。

快捷提问（Quick Suggestion/ Quick Reply）

- 样式：一个个可点击的圆角按钮或卡片
- 使用场景：冷启动页、AI 首轮问答后
- 特点：操作门槛低，固定的提示词，点击即发送
...
而且可以根据实际需求进行功能定制，比如支持多选；
...
推荐要显眼还是轻量？

冷启动场景：新用户刚进入时，推荐要足够「显眼」，避免出现“输入门槛高、不知道说什么”的尴尬。 设计策略：用卡片式、气泡式高亮推荐，给到一眼可点的操作感。...

results.summary:
# AI Chat UX: Structured Cards, Thinking Traces, and Suggestion Pills

Plain text bubbles waste the AI chat medium. Six UX patterns from production — structured cards, thinking traces, narrowing pills — and why each earns its place.

Ostap Kovalisko

Founder & AI Systems Architect

February 23, 2026•8 min read

Most AI chat interfaces are a text box and a wall of paragraphs. That made sense in 2023 when the model could only produce prose. In 2026, when your agent can query nine systems and execute actions, rendering everything as text bubbles wastes the medium. These are the six patterns we ship in production chat products, and what each one is for.

## 1. Structured Response Cards

The agent decides the shape of the response, not just the words. Ask for status across clients — you get a table. Ask what's pending — a checklist with live states. Ask the agent to do something — an action proposal card with the exact operation, target, and an approve button. Confirmations and errors get their own card types too, so success and failure are visually unambiguous.

Card type | Triggered by | Why not prose 
---|---|---
Table / report | Comparisons, status queries | Scannable in 5 seconds; prose takes 40 
Checklist | Open items, multi-step processes | States (done / pending / blocked) need icons, not adjectives 
Action proposal | Agent wants to execute something | Approval must be explicit — a button, not an interpreted "ok" 
Confirmation | Action completed | Proof of what happened, with a link to the result 
Error | Something failed | Failures buried in friendly prose get missed 

Implementation note: have the model emit typed JSON per card and render with real components. Parsing markdown-ish text into UI is a permanent source of breakage.
...
## What to Build First

- Action proposal + confirmation cards — the safety-critical pair
...
## Frequently asked questions

## When should I use a structured card instead of a plain text response?+

Use structured cards when the response contains discrete data the user will act on, such as a comparison, a record with fields, or a set of options. Plain text works for open explanation, but it wastes the medium when the content has clear structure that a card can make scannable and interactive.
...
## Are these six UX patterns worth the added build effort over simple chat bubbles?+

Each pattern is justified only when it does concrete work, such as reducing typing, exposing reasoning, or making data actionable. If a plain text bubble conveys the same value, the extra structure is not worth it, so apply these patterns selectively rather than by default.

results.summary:
This page covers declarative generative UI with json-render, a generative UI framework that defines component catalogs, generates specs with AI, and renders them safely across React, Vue, Svelte, and Angular. For Google’s A2UI specification (integrated via CopilotKit), see A2UI below.

## When to use this approach
Use declarative generative UI for the long tail of your product, where the agent can compose layouts you did not fully anticipate while staying inside a set of components you approve: secondary interactions, internal tools, and dashboards. When a surface is high-traffic or brand-critical and must be exact, move toward controlled generative UI. When you want interfaces created outside your application, move toward open-ended generative UI.

## How it works

- Define a catalog: declare what components the AI can use, with typed props
- Prompt the AI: describe the UI you want in natural language
- AI generates a spec: a JSON document describing the component tree
- Render safely: json-render’sRenderer renders the spec using your components

## Define a component catalog
The catalog describes every component the AI is allowed to use. Each component has a Zod schema for its props and a description that the AI reads to understand when to use it:
...
{
      description: "A card container with optional title and padding",
      props: z.object({
        title: z.string().optional(),
        padding: z.enum(["sm", "md", "lg"]).optional(),
...
props:
...
z.enum(["text", "email", "password", "number", "textarea"]).optional(),
...
Keep catalogs focused. Include only components the AI needs for the use case. A smaller catalog produces better results than a kitchen-sink approach.

## Build a component registry
The registry maps each catalog component to its actual rendering implementation. Use defineRegistry to get type-safe bindings between the catalog props and
your component functions:
...
## Connect to the agent
The agent uses structured output to return a json-render spec. Set up useStream
with your agent’s assistant ID, then extract the spec from the AI message’s
tool_calls:
...
## Stream and render progressively
During streaming, the spec is built up incrementally. Elements arrive one at a time and may initially lack type or props. Filter to only complete elements
and pass loading={true} to the Renderer, which tells it to silently skip
children that haven’t arrived yet. The UI builds up component by component:
...
JSONUIProvider is required to set up json-render’s internal context
providers (state, visibility, validation, actions). The Renderer component
must be rendered inside it.

## The spec format
The AI agent generates a flat JSON spec with a root key pointing to the
root element and an elements map containing all components:

Each element references its children by ID, and leaf elements like
...
TextInput
and Button have empty children arrays.

## A2UI: an alternative declarative spec
One way to describe an interface declaratively is json-render. A2UI is another: Google’s declarative, streaming-first generative UI specification, integrated via CopilotKit. Like json-render, it composes interfaces from components you register, so the agent stays inside guardrails you define. A2UI comes in two variants:
- Dynamic schema: a secondary model generates the full interface, including schema, data, and layout, from the conversation, for maximum flexibility.
- Fixed schema: the component tree is defined on the frontend and the agent streams only data into it, for the fastest and most predictable rendering.

## Best practices

- Use descriptive component descriptions: the AI uses these to understand when to use each component. Clear descriptions lead to better UI generation.
- Validate before rendering: always check that elements have validtype and
non-null props before passing to the Renderer, since streaming delivers partial data.
- Design for streaming: passloading={true} during streaming so the Renderer
gracefully handles children that haven’t arrived yet. Users see the UI build up
in real time rather than waiting for the full response.
- Style with design tokens: use CSS custom properties so rendered components adapt to light and dark themes automatically.
- Wrap with JSONUIProvider: theRenderer must be inside a JSONUIProvider
to access json-render’s internal context for state, visibility, and actions.
...
Connect these docs to your agent of choice via MCP for real-time answers.

### 12.20 Slack as an Output Channel

Slack is a first-class channel for the email agent to communicate with the user.
Many users live in Slack during the workday — pushing the morning brief and
urgent alerts there is higher-impact than an Agent-UI-only surface. This section
aligns with [Messaging Integrations](/plans/messaging-integrations-plan)
([#635](https://github.com/amd/gaia/issues/635)) but front-loads Slack for the
email agent specifically.

**Phased scope:**

| Phase | Shape | New code |

| **MVT** | Incoming Webhook (one-way push) | ~50 LOC — POST formatted brief/alert to `SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL` |
| **C1 Polish** | Slack MCP server (bidirectional read/send) | Pre-configured MCP; ~30 LOC tool-mixin glue |
| **C2** | Slack bot with interactive messages (approve/edit/reject buttons) | ~2 d — Events API handler, OAuth app, Block Kit UI |

**MVT — Incoming Webhook (default: DM-to-self):**

- User creates a Slack Incoming Webhook in their workspace (one-time, 2 min).
- User sets `SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL` via `gaia email slack-setup` or in the Agent UI
  Settings → Email → Slack.
- Agent posts Block Kit–formatted messages for:
  - Morning brief delivery (runs after local triage; user opts in per channel).
  - Urgent-message alerts (L4+ classified urgent → push within 30 s).
- Bodies are redacted by default in Slack — show sender + subject + one-line
  summary. Click-through link opens the message in the Agent UI thread view.
- No inbound from Slack. User still triages inside Gmail/Outlook or the Agent UI.

**C1 Polish — Slack MCP Server:**

- Pre-configure a Slack MCP server template in `mcp_servers.json` alongside
  Gmail/Outlook. Candidates: `@modelcontextprotocol/server-slack` (Anthropic
  reference) or active community alternatives — decision in §24 Q15.
- Agent gains `send_slack_message`, `read_channel`, `search_slack` tools auto-
  registered via `MCPClientMixin`.
- User can DM GaiaAgent in Slack: "what's urgent?" → agent queries local Gmail
  MCP, classifies, replies in-thread. This reuses the messaging-adapter
  restricted tool set ([Security Model](/plans/security-model) §12.2) — Slack DMs
  cannot trigger email sends without an explicit confirm in the Agent UI.

**C2 — Interactive Approval Flow:**

- Full Slack app (OAuth + Events API + Block Kit).
- Agent drafts a reply → posts to Slack with `[Approve] [Edit] [Reject]`
  buttons. Approve = send via Gmail MCP. Edit = opens thread in Agent UI. Reject
  = discard.
- Scheduled brief delivery via the autonomy engine
  ([autonomy-engine.mdx](/plans/autonomy-engine)) — runs T0/T1/T2 cascade, posts
  structured brief to Slack.
- Hooks into Agent Inbox (§12.6): Slack-driven approvals write to the same
  ledger as UI-driven approvals; undo works across both.

**Content formatting:**

- Block Kit with sections for Urgent / Actionable / Informational / Archived.
- Plain-text fallback for narrow clients.
- Char limit: 4,000 per block, truncate long summaries with "…" + click-through.
- Emoji prefixes for triage buckets (🔥 urgent, 📬 actionable, ℹ️ info,
  🗃️ auto-archived).

**Security (extends [Security Model](/plans/security-model) §12):**

- **Slack token** stored in credential vault (C2) or `~/.gaia/email/slack.json`
  (chmod 600) for MVT/C1. Treated as a secret; log-redacted.
- **Webhook URL** is also a secret (anyone with the URL can post). Same storage
  and redaction rules.
- **Workspace admin visibility** — in managed workspaces, admins may see
  messages. The Settings UI warns users and recommends personal workspaces or a
  compliance review before enabling on work Slack....

results.title: The End of "Chat": Why AI Interfaces Must Be Polymorphic - DEV Community
results.summary:
Stop forcing your AI to just talk. Let it build.

If you are building AI agents today, you are likely stuck in the Text Trap.

You build a sophisticated agent that can query databases, analyze live telemetry, or debug code. But then you force it to squeeze all that rich intelligence into a single, lossy format: A chat bubble.

- User: "How’s the server latency?"
- Agent: "The server latency is currently high, peaking at 2000ms..."

This is a UI failure.

If a human engineer saw that latency spike, they wouldn't write a paragraph about it. They would look at a Line Chart. If they found a bug in the code, they wouldn't explain it in a chat window; they would fix it directly in the IDE via Ghost Text.

We need to stop treating AI as a chatbot and start treating it as a Polymorphic Engine.

## The Concept: Just-in-Time UI

I recently implemented a system I call Polymorphic Output. The core philosophy is simple: If input can be anything (multimodal), output must be anything.

The Agent shouldn't just generate text; it should generate Intent and Data. The Interface Layer then decides—in real-time—how to render that data based on the user's context.

- Context: Chat Window → Output: Text/Cards
...
IDE → Output: Ghost Text/Diffs
...
Dashboard → Output: Live Widget
...
Critical Alert → Output: Toast Notification

## The Architecture

The implementation (which you can find in the [linked repo]) separates the "Brain" from the "View."

### 1. The Modality Detector

Instead of a simplereturn string, the agent passes its response through an OutputModalityDetector. This module analyzes two things: Data Type and Urgency.

- Is it time-series data? →Modality.CHART

- Is it tabular data? →Modality.TABLE

- Is it a code fix? →Modality.GHOST_TEXT

- Is the urgency > 0.9? →Modality.NOTIFICATION

### 2. The Generative UI Engine

This is where the magic happens. The engine takes the raw data and the modality hint, and generates a UI Component Specification.

This isn't a hard-coded React component. It's a JSON description of a UI that should exist.
{
  "component_type": "DashboardWidget",
  "props": {
    "title": "API Latency",
    "value": "2000ms",
    "trend": "up",
    "alertLevel": "critical"
  },
  "style": {
    "borderLeft": "4px solid #FF0000"
  }
}

Your frontend (React, Flutter, etc.) simply reads this JSON and renders the component.

## Real-World Scenarios

Here is how this changes the user experience:

### Scenario A: The DevOps Dashboard

Old Way: You ask the bot "Show me errors." It replies with a text list of log lines. You have to read them.
Polymorphic Way: You ask "Show me errors." The agent detects a stream of error logs. It switches modality toDASHBOARD_WIDGET. A live, red-bordered widget appears on your screen, updating in real-time.

### Scenario B: The IDE Copilot
...
You ask "Fix this bug." The bot replies in a side window: "You should change line 42 to..."
...
You ask "Fix this bug." The agent detects it is inside an IDE context. It switches toGHOST_TEXT. The solution appears directly in your editor as a gray suggestion. You hit Tab to accept.

### Scenario C: The Data Analyst
...
Get me the top 10 users." Bot returns a Markdown list.
...
The agent detects tabular data. It renders an Interactive Table. You can click the headers to sort bycreated_at or filter by 

## The Startup Opportunity: Generative UI SDKs

There is a massive gap in the market right now for a Generative UI SDK.

Developers are tired of hard-coding every single screen, form, and chart. They want to drop in a library that takes Agent Output and automatically renders the perfect UI.

Imagine an SDK where you write:
# The agent just returns data
response = agent.run("Show me sales trends")

# The SDK decides it needs a Bar Chart and renders it
ui.render(response) 

No manual parsing. No building specific chart components. Just data in, UI out.

## Conclusion

We are moving away from "Chat" and...

results.title: Chat Interface Dark UX Pattern | Structured UI Guide
results.summary:
A UX designer on r/UXDesign with 20+ years of experience building AI chat interfaces put it perfectly: “It’s like a CLI, but worse as there’s no manual, and you have to explore and fail a lot (all while being charged, very often). I tend to think this is why it’s adopted; the engineers still LOVE the command line.”

That last sentence hits. The chat interface is an engineer’s UI that shipped to everyone.

I’ve talked to dozens of founders building AI products. The ones who default to chat almost always say the same thing: “We’ll add more structure later.” But later never comes because chat becomes the product’s identity. Users form habits around it. Your support docs are all about prompting. Your onboarding teaches people how to talk to your product instead of teaching them what your product can do for them. It calcifies.
...
## Why Chat Won (and Why That’s a Problem)

Let me be fair for a second. Chat wasn’t a conspiracy. It became the default AI interface for legitimate reasons:

- LLMs generate text. Chat is the natural container for text generation.
- It requires zero information architecture decisions upfront.
- It feels magical in demos. Investors love watching someone type a sentence and get a paragraph back.
- It shipped fast. No forms to design, no state to manage, no edge cases to handle.

But “ships fast” and “serves users well” are different things. And the gap between them is where your users fall off.

One commenter on r/UXDesign nailed the distinction: “This is a stretch of the term ‘dark pattern’. There’s no deliberate deception here. Chat was just the natural best fit for a technology that essentially generates text. I think you have valid critiques but they’re not ‘dark patterns’, more like misaligned expectations and lack of affordances.” Fair, and the wider picture of which moves earn trust and which quietly burn it is covered in AI-first product UX patterns.

Fair. Let me refine my claim. The chat interface isn’t deliberately deceptive. It’s something worse in some ways: it’s accidentally exclusionary. It works great for the 10% of users who already know how to prompt. For the other 90%, it creates what I call prompt anxiety: the feeling that you’re doing it wrong because you don’t know the magic words.

## The Learned Helplessness Problem

Slight detour, but this matters. There’s a psychological pattern called learned helplessness. It’s when people repeatedly fail at something and eventually stop trying, even when the situation changes and success becomes possible.

Chat interfaces do this to users at scale.

Think about it. A user opens your AI product. They see a blank box. They type something reasonable. The output is mediocre. They try rephrasing. Still mediocre. They try a third time with a longer prompt. Slightly better, but not what they wanted. Eventually they think: “I’m not good at this” or “this tool doesn’t work for me.”

Neither conclusion is true. The tool works fine. The user’s intent is clear. The problem is that a blank text box provides zero guidance on how to get from intent to result.

Compare this to a form that says: “What type of report? (quarterly/monthly/custom) | What data? (revenue/users/engagement) | Audience? (board/team/investors).” Same three inputs the user would’ve had to figure out how to express in natural language. But now you’ve eliminated the guessing.

## When Chat Actually Works

I’m not saying burn every chat interface. I’m saying use it for the right jobs:

Chat works when:

- The task is genuinely open-ended (creative brainstorming, debugging, exploring a new domain)
- Users don’t know what they want yet and need to think out loud
- The conversation itself is the value (therapy bots, learning tutors, pair programming)
- Your user base is technical and already comfortable with natural language interfaces

Chat fails when:

- Users repeat similar workflows (generating reports, creating content from templates, filling forms)
- The inputs are predictable and enumerable (choose from X options, set Y parameters)
- Users need to compare or iterate on outputs (structured views beat scrolling through chat history)
- Onboarding matters (a blank prompt teaches nothing about what your product can do)
- The task has a clear structure that the user shouldn’t have to discover via trial and error

If 80% of your users are doing the same five things, give them buttons...

results.title: Generative UI overview - Docs by LangChain
results.summary:
# Generative UI overview

Understand the generative UI spectrum from controlled to declarative to open-ended interfaces

Generative UI is any pattern where an agent’s output presents a user interface beyond text. Instead of streaming a paragraph into a chat bubble, the agent drives forms, cards, dashboards, and interactive controls. This lets your UI communicate results the way an application would, while the agent decides what to show and when. Generative UI is not a single technique. It spans a spectrum defined by one question: who authors the interface? At one end you write every component and the agent only chooses among them. At the other end, the interface is created entirely outside your application. Progressing along the spectrum trades predictability for expressive range.

## The generative UI spectrum
The spectrum runs from full control over every pixel to full agent autonomy, using three primary approaches:
More controlMore autonomy
Moving left to right, predictability and per-capability engineering cost both fall, while the agent’s expressive range grows. Accessibility and visual consistency are easiest to guarantee on the left and hardest to guarantee on the right.

### Controlled
You author the components, and the agent selects which one to render and what data to pass. This gives the highest predictability and the tightest control over branding and accessibility, at the cost of writing a component for every capability you want to expose. It is the workhorse of generative UI and the right fit for high-traffic, brand-critical surfaces where a layout must be exact, such as flight tickets and booking confirmations. Your component library is the boundary: the agent can only render what you shipped. Controlled generative UI covers components as tools, tool-call rendering, state rendering, and reasoning. For details, see Controlled generative UI.

### Declarative
The agent emits a structured specification, and the frontend composes the interface from a catalog of components you register ahead of time. The catalog acts as a guardrail and boundary: the agent can arrange and combine your components freely, but cannot step outside the set you approve. This is where the long tail lives. It trades pixel-perfection for breadth, which suits secondary interactions, internal tools, and dashboards where showing something useful matters more than exact control. Declarative generative UI covers this with json-render; Google’s A2UI, integrated via CopilotKit, offers the same shape with dynamic and fixed schema variants.

### Open-ended
The agent owns the canvas. The interface is created outside your application, for example by an MCP server, and rendered in a sandbox. This gives the widest expressive range and can add new interface capabilities with no frontend code on your side, which suits one-off visualizations and bespoke answers where a result that is surprising and good enough beats one that is predictable. It is also the most experimental approach: the least deterministic, and the hardest in which to guarantee accessibility, consistency, and safety, so the UI must be isolated. The sandbox and your prompt are the boundary. For details, see Open-ended generative UI.

## Choosing an approach
Start from how much you need to constrain the interface:
Choosing a single approach for an entire product is the most common mistake. Real applications mix approaches and match each surface to its purpose: controlled components for the high-traffic, brand-critical core, declarative composition for the long tail of secondary interactions, and open-ended embeds for third-party capabilities. A single session can move across all three. The spectrum also applies beyond chat. The same three approaches describe generative interfaces on mobile and in surfaces like Slack or email, not only in a chat transcript.

If you need to… | Choose 
---|---
Guarantee branding, layout, and accessibility for a known set of outputs | Controlled 
Let the agent compose novel layouts using only approved components | Declarative 
Surface interfaces authored by third parties without building them yourself | Open-ended

results.title: Beyond Chat: The Interfaces AI Actually Needs - DEV Community
results.summary:
Chat is a great demo container and a mediocre default for most work. The next wave is embedded, structured, and silent.

Elena watched her team build yet another chat interface. The third one that quarter. Each one was a text box with a model behind it, and each one was failing — not because the model was wrong, but because the interface was wrong. Chat didn't lose. It found its place: exploratory work, not operational throughput.

Here's the thing: chat imposes turn-taking on tasks that aren't dialogues. Filing expenses, approving POs, configuring systems — these want deterministic UI with AI assistance at decision points. The interface should match the mental model of the task, not the model's favorite I/O format.

3 patternsinline assist, structured wizard, background agent — cover most enterprise AI UXUX framework↓ 40%time-on-task drop we see moving high-volume workflows from chat to structured UIIllustrative — measure your flows2 weekstime to build a non-chat AI surface vs. a chat interface — comparable effort, radically different adoptionObserved across multiple product teams

## Patterns replacing default chat

- Sidecar panels — context from the page, no copy-paste theater
- Generative forms — AI proposes fields; user edits; submit is explicit
- Status rails — long jobs show progress, not typing indicators
- Approval queues — agents batch work; humans swipe approve

Interface test

Would a user know what happened if you removed the chat history? If not, the UI failed.

Task-specific UI replacing default chat — inline assist, structured wizards, background agents.

Chat is the command line of AI — powerful, beloved by builders, wrong for everyone else on most tasks.

## Chat isn't dead — it's demoted

Exploratory work still loves chat — brainstorming, unfamiliar domains, debugging when you don't know the question yet. Operational work hates it. Expense approval, ticket triage, config changes — these want buttons, validation, and undo. Design mode switches: explore in chat, execute in structure.

Task-specific affordances — forms, buttons, inline approvals — beat another chat bubble for real work.

Users blame "the AI" when the interface lied about what happened. Structured UIs show state — draft, pending approval, sent. Chat hides state in scrollback. Enterprise trust needs visible state machines, not clever prose.

- Inline assist — suggest next field value;
...
no conversation
- Batch queues — agent prepares ten drafts; human approves in list view
- Progress rails — long jobs show steps, not typing dots
- Error surfaces — red banner with retry, not apologetic paragraph

Chat is a great discovery interface and a terrible system of record.

## Measuring interface fit

Track time-on-task, error rate, and repeat usage per workflow. When structured UI beats chat by 40% on time, stop forcing conversation. A/B the shell, not just the model — UX is where enterprise AI lives or dies.

Audit your AI features — how many are chat-only because chat was fastest to ship? Pick the highest-volume workflow and reshape it as a form with AI-filled fields. Users will thank you with adoption, not praise for innovation theater.
...
Can the user complete the task without reading the chat history? That's the bar.

## Accessibility and chat

Chat UIs are notoriously bad for screen readers and async workflows. Structured forms with labels beat message bubbles for compliance and accessibility. Enterprise buyers increasingly ask — plan beyond the cool chat demo.

Design mobile-first for field workflows. Chat on a phone in a warehouse is misery; big buttons and photo capture with inline AI are productivity.

## APIs over chat for automation

Other systems need structured webhooks and APIs, not chat transcripts. Design AI features with machine-readable outputs first; chat is one consumer. B2B integrations die when the only interface is a thread.

Expose the same capability as REST event and as sidecar UI. Chat demos; APIs scale.

## Executive dashboards aren't chat

Leaders want cards, deltas, and drill-down — not a thread to scroll. Embed AI summaries in BI surfaces they already open Monday morning.

Ship one non-chat AI surface next sprint. Measure adoption against the chat feature it replaces.

## Mobile field workflows

Technicians need camera capture, big confirm buttons, offline queue — not a chat thread in sunlight on a cracked screen. Design for gloves, glare, and intermittent connectivity.

Default to structured UI for anything repeated weekly. Reserve chat for exploration and debugging. Your users aren't asking for more threads — they're asking for fewer clicks.
